rationale: Paraphrase stability is mixed: on TESS all 7/7 predictive Jev features pass rho>=0.85 and mean |dp|<=0.05 (paraphrase |dp| 0.0250 = 4.4x same-wording noise 0.0056) but 2 label-echo features fail, and on Kepler 3 of 6 predictive features fail rho (0.841, 0.828, 0.651) (RESULTS.md sec. 6; RESULTS_KEPLER.md KG3).

Laya gate (accept at p>=0.4 with word overlap or p>=0.8, else lexical fallback or LLM replan) gives 88.8% vs 92.0% for budget-matched ReAct (-3.2 pp, CI -7.7 to +1.2) at 83.6% fewer tokens, but is not significantly better than word-overlap matching (+2.3 pp, CI -0.2 to +5.0) and post-action verification never fired in 403 steps (Tables 1-2, sec. 6).

Audio-Laya reaches 99.6-100% macro-F1 on the 282-call spam split, but labels are fully confounded with source, and zero-shot direct-audio transfer to MInDS-14 is at or below the majority baseline (6.2-8.5% accuracy vs 8.5%); only the ASR-to-text Laya route reaches 93.6% (Tables 4.1-4.2, sec. 4.1).

Jev accuracy 0.961 SST-2 / 0.867 AG News beats gpt-5.4-nano (0.948/0.811) and gpt-4.1-nano (0.938/0.851) and the zero-shot -c checkpoint (+5.72 pp [4.70, 6.75]) but is below the task-exposed checkpoint on AG News (-2.30 pp [-3.33, -1.28]), and label wording alone moves the gap from +6.93 to +9.67 pp (Tables 6-8, sec. 4.3).

Calibration depends on question form and task (ECE 0.091 yes/no vs 0.020 choice on the same 872 SST-2 items; AG News 0.089, middle bins state 0.750 vs observed 0.612; 71.6% of answers at exactly 1.00) and is repaired only by fitted temperature scaling (to 0.023/0.028), whose value depends on zero-clipping (Tables 2, 4; sec. 4.1).

A 5% automatic tier certifies for Jev in 0 of 2,000 AG News splits (vs 23 for -c, 95 task-exposed) but in 191 of 2,000 on SST-2 (9.4% automation); conformal single-label answers are wrong 5.93% at nominal 5%; gpt-4.1-nano certifies 0 (raw) or 70 (renormalised) splits, so the generative comparison is convention-dependent (sec. 4.2, 4.5, 4.6; Table 5).

WEV models have ECE at or below 0.06 on browser steps (WEV-4b 0.024 Mind2Web, 0.059 NNetNav) and at or below 0.10 out of domain (0.033-0.099 transfer-v4), with a smooth DONE threshold trade-off (WEV-4b: 82% recall/8.5% premature at 0.5; 67%/3.8% at 0.8), although BLOCKED recall is only 3% (Table 7, Fig. 3, Table 10).

On 741 quote-gold RFQs Jev reaches 91.9% primary-class accuracy vs 89.6% for Qwen3.5-35B and 78.0% for Laya, but on fulfillment mode Jev 65.0% is below Qwen 71.0% (Laya 45.7%) (README Results table; report sec. 9.1, 9.3).

Nine Jev question-structure and input variants (twelve nouls, one 12-way choice, hierarchical choices x three state texts) all land between 91.2% and 91.9% on the same 741 rows, a spread of five rows within overlapping 95% intervals (report sec. 8.2-8.3).

Jev primary-class ECE is 0.046-0.052 across all nine variants (0.125 on fulfillment) while Laya ECE is 0.322 (0.41 fulfillment) with over-firing flags (text_insufficient 71-76% vs Jev 13-15%); Qwen's three confidence buckets cannot reach 95% precision (high bucket 90.1% at 97.8% coverage) (sec. 8.2, 9.1, 9.4).

With a Wilson-bounded cutoff of 0.94 set on the gold rows Jev auto-accepts 86.5% at 96.7% precision while neither Qwen nor Laya reaches a 95% cutoff at any depth; a Jev+Qwen-agreement gate automates 91.9% of 12,000 rows at 93.8% precision (sec. 9.2, 9.6).

On five public classification benchmarks including Civil Comments insult moderation, Reflex-1 averages 84.2 and Jev 83.6 vs 85.6/84.8 for GPT-5.6/Gemini 3.8, with no task training (README Results table).

Jev action probabilities report ECE 0.0228 and Brier 0.0274 on 1,000 frozen Binance ticks (Level-3 ablation ECE 0.0240) and ECE 0.042-0.048 in the 1,440-cycle live run; no generative model's calibration is measured (Abstract; Tables 2, 5).

On the 22-review, 142,504-record TITAN-SR external set Jev reaches median AUC 0.9827 and S@95R 0.9339 (TITAN-SR 0.9760/0.8970, ASReview S@95R 0.7520), with recall 0.9349 pooled and >=99% in 16/22 reviews at the untuned 0.3 threshold; comparators were not rerun and are not stated to be generative (report.md).

At a development-selected threshold (0.170 from 1,000 dev labels) Jev reaches 90.52% recall at 3.24% FPR on ToxicChat vs 35.63-58.91% for encoders, but at 0.5 recall is 77.01% and the post hoc human-annotated FPR is 5.39%, above the 5% quality bound (Tables R1, R1a, A2; sec. 7).

On 4,000 held-out names every probability band was right at least as often as Jev stated (>=0.95: 1,661 names, 99.5% right, 95% CI 99.1-99.8), i.e. conservative calibration usable for thresholding (slide 9).

Gating Jev's reranking on its probability (threshold 0.62 set on 1,000 separate names, else dksplit fallback) raises accuracy from 90.0% to 92.8% (McNemar p = 2.5e-13), and every threshold from 0.30 to 0.98 beats dksplit alone; at >=0.90, 53.1% of names are accepted at 99.2% (slides 6-8).

Jev classified 41,172 OpenAlex records for a public research panel; agreement with an 88-record agent-adjudicated set is 90.9% overall and 97.2% for the 72 records at p>=0.75, but no independent human validation exists and admitting lower-confidence labels changes the corpus by +49.8% (sec. 2.4, Tables 1, 3).

Yway transfers fully to unseen wordings on broadly worded tasks (answerable 0.92, relevance 0.86, topic 0.89) but 'has a number' falls from 0.995 to 0.579 under a slightly shifted unseen wording; off-the-shelf multilingual Laya is at chance on Burmese topics (0.120) (sec. 5.4, Fig. 7, Table 2).

After a per-question-type temperature fitted on validation, ECE is 0.006-0.035 on most tasks but 0.114 on 12-way topic, and the answer checker reaches ECE 0.013 only after training on 22,000 real judged answers (sec. 4.3, 5.1, 5.2).

As a filter the checker catches 81% of wrong answers at 0.5 while keeping 68% of correct ones (shown-answer quality 0.44 to 0.68), but only after round-3 training on real errors (synthetic negatives scored correct 0.89 vs wrong 0.91) and it judges changed-number answers correctly only 45% of the time (sec. 5.2, Figs. 4-5).

Jev chose 'maybe' on only 1.0% and 0.8% of 40,725 triples it judged from three labels with no evidence, and verdicts were not fully coherent: 7 of 46 and 4 of 127 duplicate-triple groups and 18 of 1,836 and 22 of 445 reciprocal pairs got differing verdicts; no ground truth was available (Tables 3, 8).

Laya detects intrusions well only with added fine-tuning and retrieval (fine-tuned+RAD F1 0.89 vs rule 0.66; base model 0.35); on real CIC-IDS2017 traffic SSH brute force transfers (F1 0.98-0.99, FPR 0.00) but slow port scans do not (recall 0.03-0.31 vs rule 0.43) (Tables 1, 2, 7).

In the simulated graduated response the fine-tuned+RAD detector blocks all attackers within about a minute but causes about 17 wrongful isolations and 5.5 wrongful block hours per replication (base model 146), never flags the unseen attack as Unknown, and the author keeps shadow mode with human approval (Tables 5-6, sec. 6.5).

With no evidence Jev Choice puts 0.83-0.93 on 'heads', almost all from the option word (+0.354) with key name +0.027 and position -0.015, but one 55% witness cuts this to +0.063; the open Laya shows key (+0.28) and first-position (+0.15) bias (Table 1, Table 6, sec. 4.1).

Jev Choice behaves as a step (45%->55% stated base rate moves it 0.59-0.89 vs correct 0.10; still 55x worse than normalized Noul after temperature scaling) while Noul stays within 0.014-0.026 of stated rates (held-out Brier 0.0034 vs 0.0665); the three open RLCD-style models all fail the audit (Tables 2-4, 6).

Against 650 items with >=100 human votes each, normalized Noul is closer to the human distribution than Choice (ChaosNLI Brier 0.096 vs 0.203), but Choice is worse than a uniform guess on DICES on every measure and neither primitive beats uniform on the most contested items (ChaosNLI Brier 0.135/0.321 vs 0.058) (Table 5, sec. 4.4).

Reversing the options changes Noma's answer on 9.7% [6.2, 14.8] of 186 sealed choice items and a random reorder on 7.0%, mostly on low-confidence items (mean 0.52), with accuracy 83.9% vs 84.9% (sec. 7.2).

After per-type temperature scaling the sealed-set ECE is 0.043 (confidence 84.7% vs accuracy 82.6%) but on held-out multi-step items confidence exceeds accuracy by 23 points (70.8% vs 48.2%); the abstain output separates unsupported items only when supervised (AUROC 0.82 vs 0.46) and needs a tuned threshold out of scope (Table 1, sec. 5.2, 6.2).

Thresholding works on single-pass items (most confident half 96.9%, top 80% 89.6% accurate) but a threshold below 0.9 will not catch multi-step errors, where the model is right about a third of the time at 0.5-0.9 confidence, and head disagreement detects errors worse than max probability (0.63 vs 0.82) (sec. 5.2, Fig. 5).

Both Human-Gated live Jev calls (R1, X1) were classified RECONSTRUCTED with 124/124 offline tests and FAIL_OPEN_COUNT 0, but n = 2 and reconstructability comes from the consumer-built deterministic shell, evidence preservation and Human Gate, not from the model output (README J4, J6 observations, Claim Boundaries).

Active Jev per-turn supervision resolves 62.3% vs 55.1% unsupervised on 69 SWE-bench tasks (+7.2 pp, CI -4.3 to +18.8, p = .332), but a no-message shadow arm shows a similar +8.5 pp and active vs shadow is only +1.6 pp (CI -6.5 to +9.7), so no supervision effect is resolved (Table 2).

In its own gridworld games Jev is overconfident (chosen-move probability 0.72 vs 51% optimal, ECE 0.21, Brier 0.283 worse than a 0.250 constant), as are GLiClass (ECE 0.33) and Laya (Brier worse than constant), while the chat model Qwen3.5-4B read as probabilities has ECE 0.06 and beats the constant; Jev's exam ECE is 0.06 (sec. 5.7, Fig. 6).

SignRule-Decide transfers across registers and languages unevenly: on Danish texts never seen in training coalitions 92.5%, minimum signers 86.4% but rule type 62.4%, vs Norwegian beyond-interpreter texts 99.0%/98.0%/93.0% (Table 5).

Test ECE is 0.002/0.007 only after per-type temperature scaling fitted per register on validation (H2), 10 of the 12 dangerous Austrian errors were given at confidence >=0.9, and Learn-then-Test abstention thresholds do not transfer to Denmark (observed risk 14.3% at a 5% target) (sec. 5, 7; Table 7 H2, H18).

Abstention by Learn-then-Test keeps risk at 1.3% with 99.9% coverage at a 2% target on Austria (H22 met) but fails on the unseen Danish register (14.3% risk at 5% target, H18 not met), and most dangerous errors occur at high confidence where no threshold catches them (Table 3, sec. 7, Fig. 1).
